title: The daughters
hookLine: Montaigne lost five of six daughters in infancy and wrote little of it, which readers still wonder about

cards: Here is a man who tells you about his kidney stones, his digestion, his bad memory, how he likes his meat cooked and how long he likes to sleep. Nothing seems too small or too private for his book.
Then, in one sentence, tucked inside an argument about something else, he mentions that some of his children died as babies. One sentence, and he moves on.
Readers have stopped at that sentence for a long time and asked what's underneath it.

teach.b: First, the sentence. In an early essay, Montaigne argues that much of what hurts us hurts because of the opinion we hold about it.
As an example, he says he has lost two or three children while they were still nursing, not without regret, but without great grief. That's all. Second, what sits around it.
The same writer gave a whole essay to his friend Étienne de La Boétie, and to losing him. Asked why he loved him, Montaigne says it could only be answered: because it was he, because it was I.
He could write grief, openly and at length. Here he doesn't. Third, how readers take the silence.
Some take him at his word: an honest report, from a time and place that spoke of such losses differently.

Some hear a man using his own argument as armor, saying the calm thing because the true thing was too heavy for the page. Some notice he doesn't give the number exactly, two or three, and sit with that.
Nobody can open the inside of another person's grief, and Montaigne doesn't open this one for us. Fourth, outside the book.
The man next to you on the train, the coworker who laughs easily, the grandmother who never mentions the brother she lost.
Some grief gets whole pages; some gets one sentence and a closed door. Both are real. The quiet kind asks for gentler eyes.
And if a grief of your own grows too heavy, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US you can call or text 988, and wherever you are, local emergency help is there.

how: Readers of Montaigne often pause at his one passing remark about losing children in infancy and read it in more than one way: as an honest report, or as grief held back from the page.

games.q: you're reading Montaigne and reach his one sentence about the children he lost. what does the script say readers do with it?
o: read it in more than one way, and admit no one can open his grief for him.
games.why: readers differ: an honest report, an argument used as armor, or a number he couldn't even give exactly. Montaigne doesn't open it for us.

practice: Bring to mind a grief that doesn't get talked about: someone else's, carried quietly, or your own, if that feels safe today. You don't need to open it or explain it.
Just turn toward it the way you'd sit beside someone on a bench without asking questions, and let the breath be soft around it.

wordCard.voice: The daughters. Montaigne wrote one passing sentence about losing children in infancy, and readers still wonder what that short sentence holds back. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: hidden grief. Some losses get only one sentence, and they still count. See you tomorrow.
